contradictions.question: How many generations must a bastard wait until his offspring can enter the congregation of the Lord?
contradictions.summary: Deuteronomy 23:2 bars the offspring of an illegitimate union from the assembly of YHWH for ten generations, but the genealogies of David in Matthew 1 and Luke 3 trace him back through Pharez (the son of Judah and Tamar's incestuous union) in only nine generations. The legal rule and the messianic genealogy don't line up.
contradictions.commentary:
Deuteronomy 23:2 is unambiguous in the Hebrew. The word *mamzer* gets translated "bastard" in the KJV, and the verse says no *mamzer* shall enter the congregation of YHWH "even to his tenth generation." Most lexicons (HALOT, BDB) treat *mamzer* as offspring of a forbidden union — the rabbinic tradition (m. Yebamot 4:13) narrowed it to incest and adultery, but the older Deuteronomic stratum reads as a blanket exclusion of illegitimate children and their descendants for ten generations. Genesis 38 then hands us Pharez, born to Judah from his daughter-in-law Tamar — exactly the kind of forbidden union that would qualify under any reasonable reading of *mamzer*. Matthew 1:3-5 and Luke 3:31-33 both run David's line through Pharez and count nine generations, not ten.

The apologetic harmonization runs in three directions. First, narrow the definition: Gleason Archer in his *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties* argues *mamzer* technically means "child of a mixed-cult marriage" or "offspring of a Canaanite cultic prostitute," not any illegitimate child. Second, dismiss the genealogy as schematic: Matthew is famously stylized into 14-14-14, so the apologist says you can't count generations literally. Third, claim the law applies only after Sinai, so Pharez was grandfathered in. Take your pick.

None of these hold up well. The narrow-cult-prostitute reading isn't supported by the Hebrew or by the rabbinic interpretation in m. Yebamot, which understood *mamzer* to cover incest cases like Tamar's. The schematic-genealogy defense actually concedes the contradiction by admitting Matthew's count isn't reliable, which then opens up bigger problems for using these genealogies to establish Davidic descent at all. And the "law applied later" move ignores that the Deuteronomist is presenting these laws as binding from Sinai forward — yet Boaz, David, and Solomon are all later than Sinai in the biblical chronology and are still inside the ten generations from Pharez. The plain reading of the Deuteronomic law and the plain reading of the messianic genealogy are in tension.

The critical-scholarly response is the more parsimonious one. The genealogies in Matthew and Luke were composed centuries after the Deuteronomic Code crystallized, and the authors were not running the math against Deuteronomy 23. Critical scholars (Christine Hayes on Second Temple intermarriage halakhah, Jeffrey Tigay in his JPS Deuteronomy commentary) note that Deuteronomy 23 reflects an ideology of exclusionary purity that later Second Temple texts (Ezra-Nehemiah) intensified, while the Davidic genealogy preserves an older inclusive tradition that simply didn't engage with the Deuteronomic exclusion. The contradiction is what you get when two streams of tradition get bound into the same canon without anyone reconciling them.

contradictions.question: Did any Moabite enter the congregation of the Lord?
contradictions.summary: Deuteronomy 23:3 and Nehemiah 13:1 explicitly forbid Moabites from ever entering the assembly of YHWH, but the book of Ruth makes a Moabite woman the great-grandmother of King David — placing her, and her descendants, squarely inside the congregation.
contradictions.commentary:
The Deuteronomic exclusion is categorical. Deuteronomy 23:3 says "An Ammonite or Moabite shall not enter into the congregation of the LORD; even to their tenth generation shall they not enter into the congregation of the LORD for ever." The Hebrew *ad-olam* — "forever" — closes the door tight. Nehemiah 13:1 quotes this Deuteronomic law and uses it as scriptural justification for his post-exilic purge of foreign wives. Then Ruth 1:4 and Ruth 4:13-17 hand us a Moabite woman marrying into Israel, bearing Obed, becoming the great-grandmother of David and — through Matthew 1:5 — an ancestor of Jesus.

The apologist playbook offers a few harmonizations. Walter Kaiser and the standard evangelical line argue the Deuteronomic exclusion applies only to males, leaning on rabbinic readings (m. Yebamot 8:3) that distinguish *Moabi* (male Moabite) from *Moabiyyah* (female Moabite). Others suggest Ruth's exemplary conversion ("thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God," Ruth 1:16) effectively naturalized her. A third move: Daniel Block in his NAC Judges/Ruth volume reads the law as excluding Moabites *as Moabites* but accepting them once they fully convert.

Here's where it falls apart. The male-only reading is post-hoc rabbinic legal gymnastics designed precisely to rescue David's legitimacy — Jacob Milgrom and others have noted that the Hebrew of Deuteronomy 23:3 uses standard collective language that nowhere else in the Pentateuch is restricted to males. Nehemiah 13:1-3 explicitly applies the same Deuteronomic rule to expel foreign wives, treating women as covered by the law. The conversion defense is anachronistic — the institutional category of "convert" (*ger tsedek*) is a much later development; Ruth herself never undergoes any conversion ritual the text bothers to describe.

The critical-scholarly read is straightforward. The book of Ruth is widely understood as a post-exilic novella written in deliberate tension with the exclusionary nationalism of Ezra-Nehemiah. Tamara Cohn Eskenazi, Adele Berlin, and Kirsten Nielsen have all argued that Ruth functions as a counter-text — its whole point is that a Moabite *can* be incorporated into Israel and even produce its greatest king. The contradiction with Deuteronomy 23 is not a bug; it's the book's polemical thesis. Reading the canon as a single voice flattens what is actually a debate between Israelite factions about who counts as Israel.

contradictions.question: How should the Edomites be treated?
contradictions.summary: Deuteronomy 23:7 forbids Israel from despising the Edomite because he is a brother, but later texts — 2 Kings 14, Ezekiel 25, and the entire book of Obadiah — celebrate the slaughter and complete destruction of Edom as righteous divine policy.
contradictions.commentary:
Deuteronomy 23:7 sets a baseline: "Thou shalt not abhor an Edomite; for he is thy brother." The kinship logic runs through Genesis — Edom descends from Esau, Jacob's twin — so the Deuteronomic Code carves out fraternal status for them, on par with Egyptians who get the same treatment in the next clause. Then 2 Kings 14:7 has King Amaziah killing 10,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt with the explicit narrative endorsement that he "did that which was right in the sight of the LORD." Ezekiel 25:13 has YHWH personally promising to wipe Edom out. Obadiah is one continuous oracle of Edom's annihilation. And Psalm 137:7-9 nurses the grudge into the post-exilic period.

The apologetic harmonization runs the dispensational line: Deuteronomy 23 reflects the early covenantal relationship, and the later prophetic oracles are responses to Edom's specific behavior — the Edomites celebrated and assisted Babylon's destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BCE, so they forfeited their fraternal protection. John Bergsma and Brant Pitre frame it as covenant-conditional: the brother-clause assumed mutual respect; Edom broke it; punishment follows. Iain Provan in his Kings commentary similarly argues 2 Kings 14 is just a war notice, not a divine command to commit genocide.

The defense has some textual purchase but doesn't actually fix the contradiction. Ezekiel 25:12-14 does cite Edom's vengeance as the ground for judgment, and Obadiah 10-14 explicitly references Edom's behavior at Jerusalem's fall. So yes, the prophetic texts have a stated rationale. The problem is that the rationale doesn't map onto 2 Kings 14, where Amaziah's slaughter of 10,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt happens during the ninth century BCE — about three hundred years before any Edomite involvement at the fall of Jerusalem. The Deuteronomistic Historian still calls it righteous.

The more parsimonious reading is that we have multiple competing Israelite traditions about Edom from different periods, bound together in the canon. Bert Dicou and John Bartlett have shown that pre-exilic Judah's relationship with Edom was politically complicated and shifted over centuries; the post-586 BCE bitterness reflected in Obadiah, Lamentations 4:21-22, and Psalm 137 is genuinely a later development. The Deuteronomic kinship rule reflects an older covenantal ideal; the prophetic oracles reflect raw post-exilic rage. The text doesn't reconcile them — it preserves both. That is of course a subjective opinion on the evidence, but it's the reading that doesn't require flattening the canon into a single voice.

contradictions.question: Is it OK for a divorced woman to remarry?
contradictions.summary: Deuteronomy 24:1-2 explicitly permits a divorced woman to become another man's wife, but Luke 16:18 has Jesus declaring that anyone who marries a divorced woman commits adultery — which would make the Deuteronomic permission a license for sin.
contradictions.commentary:
Deuteronomy 24:1-2 is the foundational divorce law: a man writes a bill of divorcement, hands it to his wife, sends her out, and "she may go and be another man's wife." The Hebrew is permissive, not grudging. The same passage (vv. 3-4) prohibits her from returning to the first husband, but a remarriage to a *different* man is openly sanctioned. Luke 16:18 then has Jesus saying flatly: "Whosoever putteth away his wife, and marrieth another, committeth adultery: and whosoever marrieth her that is put away from her husband committeth adultery." There is no exception clause in Luke. The Matthean parallel (Matt 5:32, 19:9) inserts the famous *porneia* exception, but Luke and Mark 10:11-12 don't.

The standard apologetic move, advanced by Craig Blomberg and David Instone-Brewer, is that Jesus is intensifying the Mosaic law for the kingdom era — he is not contradicting Deuteronomy but giving its true intent. Instone-Brewer in *Divorce and Remarriage in the Bible* argues that Jesus is targeting the Hillelite "any cause" divorces that abused the Deuteronomic permission, not banning all remarriage. Others appeal to canonical hermeneutics — earlier law gives way to later teaching as the redemptive plan unfolds.

The steel-manned version has some force in Matthew, where the *porneia* clause and the rabbinic debate context (Hillel vs. Shammai) make Instone-Brewer's reading plausible. But Luke 16:18 has no exception and no debate context. It is a flat declarative statement that anyone who marries a divorced woman commits adultery. If Jesus is merely "correcting an abuse," Luke's redactor either didn't get the memo or wasn't trying to tell that story. The contradiction with Deuteronomy 24 is structural: what Moses permits, Jesus calls adultery.

The critical-scholarly read accepts what's on the page. John P. Meier in *A Marginal Jew*, Vol. 4, argues at length that Jesus historically prohibited divorce absolutely — making him significantly stricter than Deuteronomic and Pharisaic law — and that the Matthean exception clause is a later softening by the Matthean community to accommodate communal realities. Joseph Fitzmyer reaches a similar conclusion in his Anchor commentary on Luke. The contradiction with Deuteronomy is real, intentional on Jesus' part, and represents a genuine break with Mosaic permission rather than a clarification of it. The harmonization works only if you read Matthew back into Luke, which is exactly the kind of canonical leveling source critics flag as illegitimate.

contradictions.question: Are those who obey the law cursed?
contradictions.summary: Deuteronomy 27:26 places under curse anyone who fails to confirm and do all the words of the law, while Galatians 3:10 turns that same verse on its head, claiming that everyone who relies on the works of the law is under a curse.
contradictions.commentary:
Galatians 3:10 is one of the most discussed verses in Pauline studies because Paul appears to weaponize Deuteronomy 27:26 against itself. Deuteronomy 27:26 in the Hebrew curses anyone who *does not* uphold the words of the law. Paul quotes that verse — and concludes the exact opposite: that those who *are of* the works of the law are under a curse. The plain reading of Deuteronomy promises curse for non-compliance and (in chapter 28) blessing for compliance. The plain reading of Galatians 3:10 says compliance itself is the curse-trigger.

The major apologetic harmonization is the implicit-premise reading championed by N. T. Wright, Daniel Fuller, and others: Paul assumes nobody actually keeps the whole law, so the curse of Deuteronomy 27:26 falls on everyone who tries to be justified by it. On this reading, Paul isn't contradicting Deuteronomy — he's pointing out that the curse-clause of Deuteronomy gets triggered for everyone because perfect law-keeping is impossible. James Dunn's New Perspective version frames it differently: the curse falls on those who use the law as a boundary marker excluding Gentiles, not on Torah obedience per se. Either way, Paul is supposedly not actually contradicting Moses.

The Wright-Fuller implicit-premise reading does substantial work, and it's defensible at the level of Paul's argument. But it requires importing a premise Paul never states in Galatians 3:10 — that nobody can fulfill the law. Paul in fact contradicts that premise elsewhere; in Philippians 3:6 he calls himself "blameless" with respect to the law's righteousness. Heikki Räisänen and E. P. Sanders have argued at length that Paul's actual logic in Galatians 3:10 is genuinely strained — he is making rhetorical use of Deuteronomy 27:26 in a way the original Deuteronomic author would not have endorsed. Sanders' summary in *Paul, the Law, and the Jewish People* is blunt: Paul reaches his conclusion first (Christ is the basis of righteousness, therefore not the law) and then constructs a scriptural argument that runs against the surface meaning of the texts he cites.

The critical-scholarly verdict is mixed but lands where Sanders does. Whether you call this a flat contradiction or Paul "creatively reappropriating" Deuteronomy is partly a matter of how generous you want to be to Paul's hermeneutic. But the surface-level tension is real: Deuteronomy curses non-compliance, Paul effectively curses compliance, and reconciling them requires reading silent premises into Paul's argument. That is of course a subjective opinion on the evidence — but the unstated-premise solution sits awkwardly with Paul's own claim to law-blamelessness in Philippians 3.

contradictions.question: Does God take pleasure in the death of the wicked?
contradictions.summary: Deuteronomy 28:63 explicitly says YHWH will rejoice to wipe out and destroy the disobedient just as he rejoiced to bless them, while Ezekiel 18:23 has YHWH ask rhetorically whether he has any pleasure at all in the death of the wicked — answer: no, he wants them to repent and live.
contradictions.commentary:
Deuteronomy 28:63 is one of the harshest verses in the Hebrew Bible. The Hebrew uses the verb *sus* — to rejoice, exult — and applies it symmetrically: just as YHWH rejoiced (*sas*) to be good to Israel, so he will rejoice to destroy them. The grammar makes the divine pleasure in destruction parallel to the divine pleasure in blessing. Then Ezekiel 18:23: "Have I any pleasure at all that the wicked should die? saith the Lord GOD: and not that he should return from his ways, and live?" The Hebrew there uses *chaphets* — to delight in, take pleasure in — and the answer is unambiguously no. Two verses, two different verbs, but the conceptual collision is direct: God either takes pleasure in destruction or he doesn't.

The apologetic harmonization is the rhetorical-hyperbole move. John Walton and Daniel Block read Deuteronomy 28:63 as covenant-curse genre language, designed to terrify Israel into compliance, not as a literal psychological description of YHWH. Apologists like Paul Copan in *Is God a Moral Monster?* lean on the same framing — Ancient Near Eastern treaty curses are notoriously over-the-top, and YHWH is using genre conventions, not actually savoring genocide. Ezekiel 18, on this reading, gives us the "real" divine attitude; Deuteronomy 28 just dramatizes the seriousness of covenant violation.

The genre defense has merit at the level of form criticism. The Deuteronomic curses do follow the structure of Hittite and Neo-Assyrian vassal treaties, and Moshe Weinfeld's classic work documents the parallels in granular detail. But the genre defense doesn't actually defuse the contradiction — it just relocates it. If Deuteronomy 28:63 is hyperbole, then the picture of God it presents is unreliable, which is exactly the critical claim. And the rejoice-in-destruction motif isn't confined to Deuteronomy 28: Proverbs 1:26 has Wisdom (often understood as divine) laughing at the destruction of fools, and Psalm 2:4 has God laughing at the wicked. The pleasure-in-destruction theme has too many independent attestations to be waved off as one stylized treaty curse.

The critical-scholarly read accepts the contradiction as evidence of competing theological streams. Walther Eichrodt, Jon Levenson, and more recently Yochanan Muffs have all noted that the Hebrew Bible holds together divergent portraits of YHWH — a wrathful covenant-enforcer in the Deuteronomistic tradition and a longsuffering, repentance-seeking God in the prophetic tradition (Ezekiel, Jonah, Joel). The two are not psychologically compatible without either softening the Deuteronomic language past what it says or hardening the Ezekielian language past what it says. The honest read is that ancient Israel's God was characterized differently by different traditions, and the canonical compilers preserved both.

contradictions.question: Do humans have free will?
contradictions.summary: The Bible holds together two streams: Deuteronomy 30:19 and Joshua 24:15 frame human destiny as a real moral choice ("choose life," "choose you this day"), while Romans 8-9, Ephesians 1, and a stack of other texts have God predestining individuals to salvation or damnation before the foundation of the world.
contradictions.commentary:
This contradiction sits at the center of a 1,700-year theological civil war and isn't going to get settled in a database entry. But the textual tension is real. Deuteronomy 30:19 is structured as a genuine choice — life and death are set before Israel, and Moses tells them to choose. Joshua 24:15 calls Israel to actively pick whom they'll serve. The grammar assumes the audience can do otherwise. Then you hit Romans 9:18-21, which has God hardening whom he wills, the potter making vessels of wrath and vessels of honor, and the rhetorical demand that the clay shut up and stop questioning the potter. Ephesians 1:4-5 has the elect chosen "before the foundation of the world." Acts 13:48 has "as many as were ordained to eternal life believed." The grammar there assumes the audience cannot do otherwise.

Apologetic harmonizations split along denominational lines. The Calvinist/Reformed read (Wayne Grudem, John Piper, John Frame) accepts the predestination texts at face value and argues Deuteronomy and Joshua describe the *experience* of choosing — which is real — without denying that the underlying decree is God's. The Arminian/Wesleyan read (Roger Olson, Thomas Oden) accepts the choice texts at face value and reads predestination as God's foreknowledge of free human responses (the "prescience" view), or as corporate election rather than individual. Molinists (William Lane Craig) try to split the difference with "middle knowledge" — God knows what you would freely do in every possible circumstance and actualizes the world he wants from that knowledge.

Each harmonization requires sophisticated philosophical machinery the biblical authors plainly did not possess. The Calvinist read empties the choice-language of meaningful content — if your choice is decreed, the imperative "choose life" reduces to theater. The Arminian prescience read empties the predestination language of its temporal priority — Romans 9:11 explicitly says the children were elected "not yet born, neither having done any good or evil," which is hard to square with election based on foreseen choices. Molinism solves the problem by stipulating an entire metaphysical category Scripture nowhere mentions.

The critical-scholarly read is more parsimonious: the biblical authors held different views on the question. Deuteronomistic theology assumes covenantal moral agency. Pauline theology, especially in Romans 9-11, develops a hard-edged predestination doctrine partly to explain why most Jews didn't accept Jesus as messiah. James D. G. Dunn, E. P. Sanders, and Heikki Räisänen all read Romans 9 as Paul wrestling with a specific historical problem (Jewish unbelief) using deterministic language he wouldn't apply consistently elsewhere — note Romans 10:9-13 where salvation hinges on confession and belief. The text contains both streams because Paul is not a systematic theologian and the Hebrew Bible isn't a single author. The systematic theologians invented determinism-vs-free-will to force coherence; the biblical writers didn't have that problem because they didn't try to reconcile it.

contradictions.question: Was Moses in good mental and physical health at age 120?
contradictions.summary: Deuteronomy 34:7 says Moses' eye was not dim and his natural force was not abated when he died at 120, but Deuteronomy 31:2 — three chapters earlier — has Moses himself say that at 120 he can no more go out and come in.
contradictions.commentary:
Two verses, same age, same person, opposite assessments. Deuteronomy 34:7: "Moses was an hundred and twenty years old when he died: his eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated." The Hebrew *lo nas lecho* — literally "his moisture had not fled" — is a vigorous-vitality idiom. Then back at Deuteronomy 31:2, Moses himself says: "I am an hundred and twenty years old this day; I can no more go out and come in." The phrase "go out and come in" is military-leadership idiom (cf. Numbers 27:17, 1 Samuel 18:13-16) — it means he can no longer lead Israel in battle.

The apologetic harmonization, articulated by Gleason Archer and Daniel Block, distinguishes between the *general* health described in Deut 34:7 (eyesight intact, vitality preserved) and the *specific* leadership-fitness disclaimer in Deut 31:2. Moses isn't saying he's physically failing; he's saying he's stepping aside for the next generation. Peter Craigie in his NICOT commentary takes a similar line — "go out and come in" is institutional, not biological. Some rabbinic readings (Rashi, Ibn Ezra) suggest Moses is being deliberately humble or simply citing the divine prohibition against entering the land (cf. the second half of 31:2: "the LORD hath said unto me, Thou shalt not go over this Jordan").

This harmonization actually has decent textual support. The military idiom reading is well-attested, and Deut 31:2 does include the divine prohibition as Moses' explanation. The two verses are not strictly logically incompatible — a vigorous 120-year-old can decline a military command. But it's hardly a slam dunk. The natural sense of "I can no more go out and come in" in proximity to "I am 120 years old this day" reads as a statement about age-related decline; the divine prohibition gets added as a second reason, not the only reason. The contradiction here is a soft one — more a tension than a flat collision.

The critical-scholarly read goes a different direction entirely. Deuteronomy 34 is widely assigned to a different stratum than Deuteronomy 31 — most source critics (Martin Noth, Richard Friedman, Jeffrey Tigay) treat Deut 34 as containing the closing notice from a Priestly or post-Deuteronomistic redactor while Deut 31 belongs to the older Deuteronomic core. The two passages were composed by different hands at different times and were never meant to be measured against each other for medical consistency. Friedman's *Bible with Sources Revealed* assigns Deut 34:1-12 partly to P and partly to a Deuteronomistic Historian editor; the eulogistic vigor-at-120 line is the kind of legendary embellishment that accumulates around founder figures over centuries. The historical Moses, if there was one, is invisible behind the canonical seams.

contradictions.question: Did the Centurion ask Jesus directly to help his servant?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 8:5-8 has the centurion personally approach Jesus and dialogue with him directly, while Luke 7:1-7 has the centurion send Jewish elders and then friends as intermediaries, explicitly saying he did not consider himself worthy to come in person.
contradictions.commentary:
This is one of the cleanest synoptic discrepancies in the Gospels. Matthew 8:5: a centurion comes to Jesus, speaking to him directly. Verses 6-8 are a face-to-face dialogue. Luke 7:3-7: the centurion sends Jewish elders to Jesus, then sends friends with the famous "I am not worthy" speech, and the text explicitly says "neither thought I myself worthy to come unto thee." In Matthew, the centurion shows up. In Luke, he deliberately stays away.

The standard apologetic harmonization, advanced by D. A. Carson and Craig Blomberg, leans on the legal principle *qui facit per alium facit per se* — "he who acts through another acts himself." On this reading, Matthew is using the ancient convention by which what an agent does counts as the principal's action; Luke is filling in the diplomatic detail. So Matthew's "the centurion came" really means "the centurion approached Jesus through his representatives," and there is no contradiction. Robert Stein and Darrell Bock take similar positions in their Luke commentaries.

The agency principle is real in ancient Mediterranean culture, and the harmonization isn't crazy. Rabbinic literature does treat agents as legal extensions of principals (m. Berakhot 5:5: "a man's agent is as himself"). But applying it to Matthew 8 strains hard. Matthew 8:7 has Jesus respond to the centurion in direct speech — "I will come and heal him" — and verse 8 has the centurion answer with the famous "speak the word only" line. This is back-and-forth dialogue narration. If Matthew were using agency-convention, you'd expect the kind of mediated phrasing Luke actually provides; instead Matthew's narrative grammar treats the centurion as physically present.

The critical-scholarly read frames this through the Synoptic Problem. Both Matthew and Luke share this story, and neither of its parallels is in Mark — meaning it comes from Q (the hypothetical sayings source) or oral tradition. Joseph Fitzmyer, John Nolland, and Ulrich Luz argue that Matthew compressed the narrative for theological effect (centering Jesus' encounter with Gentile faith) while Luke expanded it with the embassies to highlight Jewish-Gentile mediation, a recurring Lukan theme. The two evangelists shaped the same underlying tradition for different purposes. The harmonization is technically possible if you stretch the agency principle past where it normally goes, but the simpler explanation is that the Gospel authors were not concerned with the kind of journalistic precision the harmonization presupposes.

contradictions.question: Who is the Lord of this world?
contradictions.summary: The Hebrew Bible repeatedly affirms YHWH as sovereign over all the kingdoms and the whole earth, but several New Testament passages — most notably the Temptation narrative and 2 Corinthians 4:4 — call Satan the "prince of this world" or "god of this world" with the kingdoms of the world apparently in his gift.
contradictions.commentary:
The Old Testament texts are univocal. From Joshua 2:11 through Psalm 47, Daniel 4:17, and Isaiah 37:16, YHWH alone is God of all the kingdoms of the earth. Then the New Testament drops in some startling counter-language. Matthew 4:8-9 and Luke 4:5-7 have Satan offer Jesus "all the kingdoms of the world," and crucially, Jesus does not deny Satan's possession of them — he refuses the deal on different grounds. John 12:31, 14:30, and 16:11 call Satan "the prince of this world" (*ho archon tou kosmou toutou*). 2 Corinthians 4:4 calls him "the god of this world" (*ho theos tou aionos toutou*). Ephesians 2:2 calls him "the prince of the power of the air."

The apologetic harmonization, defended by D. A. Carson and Murray J. Harris, distinguishes between *de jure* and *de facto* sovereignty. YHWH is the rightful king of the cosmos; Satan is a usurper currently exercising influence over the fallen world by divine permission. So God remains "Lord" in the metaphysical sense while Satan is the functional ruler of this present evil age — a temporary state that ends at the eschaton. Greg Boyd in *God at War* leans even harder into the warfare worldview, arguing the Bible consistently presents the cosmos as contested territory.

The two-tier sovereignty defense actually has Pauline support — Paul's apocalyptic framework (Rom 8:38, 1 Cor 2:8, Gal 1:4) does treat "this present evil age" as dominated by hostile powers under divine sufferance. So at the level of New Testament theology, this is a coherent move. But it doesn't actually map back onto the Hebrew Bible material, which simply doesn't have the *de jure / de facto* distinction. When Joshua 2:11 says YHWH is God in heaven above and earth beneath, the Deuteronomistic Historian is not setting up a category for "another god currently runs the kingdoms." The two-stage sovereignty is a theological development of the Second Temple period, not a feature of pre-exilic Israelite thought.

The critical-scholarly read places this contradiction inside the development of Jewish demonology. Paolo Sacchi, John J. Collins, and Larry Hurtado have traced how Second Temple apocalyptic — 1 Enoch, the Qumran Community Rule, *Jubilees* — developed an increasingly elaborate cosmic dualism in which fallen angelic powers (Belial, Mastema, eventually Satan) were assigned authority over the present age. The New Testament absorbs this apocalyptic framework, then applies it to Jesus' work. So "prince of this world" is not a reading you can extract from the Hebrew Bible; it's a Second Temple development that the New Testament authors retrofit onto older monotheistic claims. The Hebrew Bible says one thing, the Synoptics and Pauline corpus say another, and the harmonization works only if you privilege the later framework as a legitimate development rather than a contradiction.

contradictions.question: Did Joshua remove the twelve stones from the Jordan River?
contradictions.summary: Joshua 4:20 says the twelve stones taken out of the Jordan were set up at Gilgal, but Joshua 4:9 — fifteen verses earlier — says the twelve stones were set up in the midst of the Jordan and "are there unto this day."
contradictions.commentary:
This is a clean doublet within a single chapter. Joshua 4:1-8 describes the twelve men, one from each tribe, taking twelve stones out of the Jordan. Verse 8 says they carried them over and laid them down. Verse 9 then says: "And Joshua set up twelve stones in the midst of Jordan, in the place where the feet of the priests which bare the ark of the covenant stood: and they are there unto this day." Then verse 20 doubles back: "And those twelve stones, which they took out of Jordan, did Joshua pitch in Gilgal." Two sets of twelve stones, or one set in two places — the text is internally muddled.

The apologetic harmonization runs the two-monuments reading. Gleason Archer, Richard Hess, and David Howard argue Joshua 4 describes two distinct memorials: one set of twelve stones brought up from the Jordan and set up at Gilgal (vv. 1-8, 20-24), and a second set of twelve stones taken from the bank and set up in the midst of the Jordan as a separate memorial (v. 9). On this reading, there is no contradiction — there are simply two monuments, and the narrative is just compressed.

The two-monuments read is the consensus harmonization and it isn't crazy. The Hebrew of verse 9 does say "Joshua set up" without specifying which stones, leaving room for a different set than the ones the twelve men carried. But the natural reading still strains. Verse 20 specifies "those twelve stones, *which they took out of Jordan*" — and that demonstrative pronoun points back at the only set of twelve stones the chapter has narrated. If verse 9 is introducing a brand-new second monument, the narrative does it abruptly with no transition. Most older critical commentators (Hertzberg, Soggin, Boling) read the doublet as evidence of redactional layering rather than two intentional monuments.

The critical-scholarly read goes to source criticism. J. Alberto Soggin and Robert Boling in their commentaries argue Joshua 4 weaves together two parallel etiological traditions about a single set of stones — one at Gilgal (the cultic site), one in the Jordan (a ford-related landmark) — and the redactor harmonized them into a single narrative without smoothing the seams. The phrase "unto this day" in v. 9 is a classic etiological marker; both verses are explaining why monuments existed at named locations in the redactor's day. The contradiction is the residue of merging two stories. The two-memorials harmonization is technically permissible but reads as a salvage operation; the doublet hypothesis explains the textual oddities more parsimoniously.

contradictions.question: Did the city of Ai exist after Joshua destroyed it?
contradictions.summary: Joshua 8:28 says Joshua burned Ai and made it "an heap for ever, even a desolation unto this day," but Nehemiah 7:32 lists 123 men of Bethel and Ai among those returning from Babylonian exile — meaning a populated Ai existed roughly a thousand years later.
contradictions.commentary:
The textual claim in Joshua 8:28 is absolute. The Hebrew *tel olam* — "a heap forever" — is permanent ruin language, and the etymological wordplay is explicit: *Ai* itself means "ruin" or "heap." Joshua 8:28 is essentially saying the place will be a permanent ruin and no one will live there. Then Nehemiah 7:32 lists "the men of Bethel and Ai, an hundred twenty and three" returning from exile in the fifth century BCE. Ezra 2:28 has the same census. So Ai was sufficiently populated under Persian rule to send 123 men to the post-exilic restoration list.

The apologetic harmonization runs along two lines. First, the topographical-rebuild line: Kenneth Kitchen, Richard Hess, and apologists generally argue Ai was rebuilt at some later point and the "forever" of Joshua 8:28 is hyperbole or applies only to a defined period. Second, the wrong-Ai line: there might have been more than one settlement called Ai (since the word just means "ruin"), and post-exilic Ai is a different site than Joshua's Ai. John Bimson and others have proposed alternative identifications.

Both defenses run into trouble. The hyperbole defense empties "forever" of meaning — and Joshua's rhetoric throughout the Conquest narratives uses similar permanence language elsewhere that apologists treat as literal when convenient. The two-Ai theory doesn't have textual support: Nehemiah pairs "Bethel and Ai" as adjacent settlements, exactly the same pairing as in Genesis 12:8 and Joshua 7-8, where Ai is east of Bethel near Beth-aven. Geographically and textually, the post-exilic Ai is the same site as Joshua's Ai.

The deeper critical-scholarly problem is that *neither* claim survives archaeology cleanly. The standard identification of Ai is et-Tell, excavated by Joseph Callaway and others, which shows the city was destroyed around 2400 BCE — well before any plausible date for Joshua — and was unoccupied during the Late Bronze Age when the Conquest narrative is set. So Ai wasn't a city Joshua could have destroyed; it was already a ruin in his (legendary) time. William Dever and Israel Finkelstein have used this as part of the broader case that the Joshua Conquest narrative is etiological — explaining existing ruins by retrojecting an Israelite military hero who "made" them ruins. On that read, the contradiction with Nehemiah resolves into a different and worse problem: Joshua 8 is folk-historical etiology, not history. Apologetic site-identifications (Khirbet el-Maqatir, championed by Bryant Wood) attempt to dodge the archaeology by relocating Ai, but mainstream archaeology has not been persuaded.

contradictions.question: Has the sun ever stood still in the sky for 24 hours?
contradictions.summary: Joshua 10:12-13 narrates the sun and moon standing still for about a full day so Joshua could finish slaughtering the Amorites, while Genesis 8:22 has YHWH promise that as long as the earth remains, day and night shall not cease — implying the regular celestial cycle is unbroken.
contradictions.commentary:
The contradiction here is between a narrative miracle and a theological promise. Joshua 10:13: "And the sun stood still, and the moon stayed, until the people had avenged themselves upon their enemies. ... So the sun stood still in the midst of heaven, and hasted not to go down about a whole day." Genesis 8:22, the post-Flood Noahic covenant: "While the earth remaineth, seedtime and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night shall not cease." Joshua 10 stops the day-night cycle for about 24 hours; Genesis 8 says it won't cease while earth endures.

The apologetic harmonization is straightforward: "shall not cease" doesn't mean "shall not be temporarily paused." John Walton, John Sailhamer, and Kenneth Mathews argue Genesis 8:22 establishes a long-term ordinance, not a guarantee of unbroken continuity at every moment. A 24-hour anomaly within an otherwise stable system doesn't violate the promise. Some apologists (Hugh Ross) reach further and reinterpret Joshua 10's "sun stood still" as a localized atmospheric phenomenon, an extended twilight, or a poetic description of cooler temperatures during a hailstorm — anything that doesn't require literally stopping celestial mechanics.

The pause-vs-cease distinction is the strongest harmonization, and at the level of textual logic it isn't unreasonable. Genesis 8:22's *lo yishbotu* ("shall not cease") could plausibly be read as a long-term ordinance that allows for miraculous interventions. The harder problem is that the whole construction of the Joshua 10 miracle assumes a pre-Copernican geocentric cosmos in which the sun and moon physically move across a fixed firmament. Joshua 10:12 has Joshua command the sun to stand *still in Gibeon* and the moon in the valley of Aijalon — directing celestial bodies as if they're chariots. The internal physics of the miracle are incoherent on any modern cosmological understanding. Ross's localized-phenomenon reading abandons the surface meaning of the text to rescue plausibility.

The critical-scholarly read is that Joshua 10:12-13 is poetic — it cites the lost "Book of Jashar" (*sefer ha-yashar*) as its source, indicating the verses are quoting ancient war poetry. Robert Boling, J. Alberto Soggin, and Richard Nelson all read the original verse as a battle-poem fragment that the prose narrator then expanded into a literal miracle ("about a whole day"). The poetic source probably described the day as unusually long in the way English speakers say "the longest day of my life" — a hyperbolic battle memorial. The literal-24-hours reading is the prose redactor's retrojection. The contradiction with Genesis 8:22 only emerges when both texts are flattened to literal historical reportage, which is exactly what the genre-critical reading rejects.

contradictions.question: Did Joshua kill everyone in Gezer?
contradictions.summary: Joshua 10:33 says Joshua smote Horam king of Gezer and his people "until he had left him none remaining," but Judges 1:29 says Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites who dwelt in Gezer, who continued living among them.
contradictions.commentary:
The Joshua text uses the strongest extermination formula in the Hebrew Bible vocabulary. Joshua 10:33: "Then Horam king of Gezer came up to help Lachish; and Joshua smote him and his people, until he had left him none remaining." The Hebrew *blti hish'ir-lo sarid* — "until none remained for him" — is the standard *herem* (devoted destruction) total-annihilation language. Then Judges 1:29: "Neither did Ephraim drive out the Canaanites that dwelt in Gezer; but the Canaanites dwelt in Gezer among them." The plain reading: Joshua exterminated everyone, then a generation later there were still Canaanites living there.

The apologetic harmonization is the partial-victory reading. Daniel Block in his NAC Judges/Ruth commentary, K. Lawson Younger, and Richard Hess argue Joshua 10:33 records the defeat of Horam's relief force — the king and his soldiers who came up to help Lachish — not the population of the city of Gezer itself. On this reading, the army got wiped out in the field; the city remained populated and was simply not occupied by Israel. The Judges 1:29 notice then describes the longer-term failure to actually take and hold Gezer.

This defense has real merit. The Joshua 10:33 verse is structurally about Horam coming up to *help Lachish*, and the "smote him and his people" phrase can plausibly be read as referring to the king and his accompanying forces, not the entire population of Gezer. Joshua never narrates an attack on Gezer city itself in the conquest sequence — Lachish gets taken in v. 32, then the relief force is destroyed in v. 33. So at the level of careful exegesis, Joshua 10:33 may not actually claim total population annihilation.

Where it gets harder is the broader narrative theology. Joshua 11:23 declares: "So Joshua took the whole land, according to all that the LORD said unto Moses... and the land rested from war." Joshua 21:43-45 reinforces it: "there failed not ought of any good thing which the LORD had spoken." Then Judges 1 systematically catalogs every place Israel failed to take or failed to drive out the inhabitants — Gezer, Bethshean, Taanach, Megiddo, Aijalon, the entire Philistine plain. The contradiction isn't really at the level of Gezer alone; it's between the totalizing rhetoric of Joshua and the partial-conquest reality of Judges 1. Source critics (Martin Noth, Frank Moore Cross, Richard Nelson) read this as evidence that the Deuteronomistic Historian wove together two competing accounts: an idealized total-conquest narrative and a more piecemeal regional-settlement tradition; the archaeological picture (Israel Finkelstein and others) lines up with the Judges 1 settlement model. Archaeology supports the Judges 1 picture — Gezer shows continuous Canaanite occupation throughout the Late Bronze and into Iron I — and Solomon eventually receives Gezer as a wedding gift from Pharaoh after he destroys the Canaanites there (1 Kings 9:16). The contradiction within the canon is real; Gezer is a small piece of a much larger seam.

contradictions.question: When was King Jabin killed?
contradictions.summary: Joshua 11:10-11 has Joshua kill Jabin king of Hazor and burn the city during the Conquest, but Judges 4:2-24 has the Israelites being oppressed by — and finally defeating — Jabin king of Hazor in the time of Deborah and Barak, generations after Joshua's death.
contradictions.commentary:
Two Jabins, two destructions of Hazor, two narratives that read like duplicates of each other. Joshua 11:1-11 has Jabin king of Hazor lead a northern coalition against Israel; Joshua kills him, slaughters everyone in Hazor, and burns the city. Then Judges 4:2 reintroduces "Jabin king of Canaan, that reigned in Hazor" oppressing Israel for 20 years, with Deborah and Barak finally breaking his power; Judges 4:24 says Israel "prevailed against Jabin the king of Canaan, until they had destroyed Jabin king of Canaan." Same name, same city, same destruction, separated by at least a generation in the narrative chronology.

The apologetic harmonization is the dynastic-name reading. Daniel Block, K. Lawson Younger, and Trent Butler argue "Jabin" was a dynastic title or a recurring royal name in Hazor, much like "Pharaoh" in Egypt or "Abimelech" in Philistine literature. So Joshua's Jabin and Deborah's Jabin are different historical kings of the same dynasty. The Hazor destruction is framed similarly: cities get rebuilt and re-destroyed; Joshua's Hazor and Deborah's Hazor are different occupational layers. Hess and Provan take this line.

The dynastic-name read isn't unreasonable in principle — multiple ancient Near Eastern dynasties did reuse throne names. The problem is the textual specifics. Joshua 11:10 calls Hazor "the head of all those kingdoms" before Joshua burns it; Judges 4 has Hazor functioning as the head of all those kingdoms again, oppressing Israel. The Joshua narrative emphasizes total destruction ("there was not any left to breathe"); the Judges narrative shows Hazor running a 900-chariot army against Israel two centuries later. If Hazor was wiped out, how does it become a regional power again so quickly?

The critical-scholarly read goes hard on the doublet hypothesis. Yigael Yadin's excavations at Hazor showed that the Late Bronze Age city was destroyed by fire around 1230 BCE, which fits a single major destruction event rather than two. Most critical commentators (Boling, Soggin, Nelson) treat Joshua 11 and Judges 4 as parallel traditions about the same conflict — a major Israelite-Canaanite battle in northern Galilee — that became attached to two different leader cycles (the Joshua cycle and the Deborah cycle) and got preserved separately in the canon. Amnon Ben-Tor's more recent excavations have refined the dating but support the single-destruction picture. The contradiction is the result of redactional preservation of competing traditions, not of two separate Hazor kings named Jabin oppressing Israel a century apart. The dynastic-name harmonization is technically permissible but archaeologically and source-critically less parsimonious.

contradictions.question: Who drove the Anakim from Hebron?
contradictions.summary: Joshua 11:21 says Joshua himself cut off the Anakim from Hebron, Debir, and the surrounding mountains and "destroyed them utterly with their cities," but Joshua 15:13-14 says Caleb drove the three sons of Anak out of Hebron.
contradictions.commentary:
Two narratives in the same book name two different conquerors of the Anakim at Hebron. Joshua 11:21: "Joshua, and cut off the Anakims from the mountains, from Hebron, from Debir, from Anab, and from all the mountains of Judah... Joshua destroyed them utterly with their cities." Joshua 15:13-14: "And Caleb drove thence the three sons of Anak, Sheshai, and Ahiman, and Talmai, the children of Anak." Same place (Hebron), same population (Anakim/sons of Anak), different conqueror. Judges 1:10 then gives a third version with the tribe of Judah doing the conquering.

The apologetic harmonization is the corporate-leadership reading. Richard Hess, David Howard, and the standard evangelical commentaries argue Joshua 11:21 is summary language describing the overall conquest under Joshua's command, while Joshua 15:13-14 zooms in on Caleb's specific role within that broader campaign. Joshua led the army; Caleb personally took Hebron as his designated allotment. There's no contradiction — Joshua 11 reports the operation at the strategic level, Joshua 15 at the tactical level. Younger and Butler take similar positions.

The corporate-leadership reading has surface plausibility. Ancient Near Eastern war narratives do sometimes credit kings or commanders with victories actually executed by subordinates. But the specifics push back. Joshua 11:22 closes the Joshua-as-conqueror passage by saying "There was none of the Anakims left in the land of the children of Israel: only in Gaza, in Gath, and in Ashdod, there remained." The narrative claims Joshua finished the job. Then Joshua 15:14 has Caleb driving out the three sons of Anak — *after* Joshua already wiped them out. And Judges 1:20 doubles back yet again with: "And they gave Hebron unto Caleb, as Moses said: and he expelled thence the three sons of Anak." So we have three different attestations of who-took-Hebron-and-when, all using slightly different formulations.

The critical-scholarly read is the source-and-tradition layering picture. Martin Noth, Robert Boling, and J. Alberto Soggin treat Joshua 11:21-23 as a Deuteronomistic summary that idealizes Joshua's conquest, while Joshua 15:13-19 preserves an older Calebite tribal tradition originally independent from the all-Israel conquest narrative. Judges 1:1-21 then preserves a third stratum, often credited to a more realistic post-conquest source. The Calebite tradition (older) credits Caleb; the Deuteronomistic summary (later) folds everything into Joshua's leadership; the redactor preserved both without smoothing them. Niels Peter Lemche and Israel Finkelstein have argued the Calebite material reflects independent southern hill-country traditions later absorbed into the all-Israel conquest schema. The harmonization is technically possible but the doublet pattern across multiple books is more parsimoniously explained by independent traditions than by repeated zoom-ins on the same event.

contradictions.question: To whom were the cities of Eshtaol and Zoreah given?
contradictions.summary: Joshua 15:20, 33 lists Eshtaol and Zoreah among the inheritance of the tribe of Judah, but Joshua 19:40-41 — four chapters later, in the same book — assigns the same two cities to the tribe of Dan.
contradictions.commentary:
The two assignments are unambiguous. Joshua 15:33: "And in the valley, Eshtaol, and Zoreah, and Ashnah" — listed within "the inheritance of the tribe of the children of Judah" (15:20). Joshua 19:40-41: "And the seventh lot came out for the tribe of the children of Dan according to their families. And the coast of their inheritance was Zorah, and Eshtaol" — listed within Dan's allotment. Same two towns, two different tribes, in the same book.

The apologetic harmonization is the geographical-overlap reading. Richard Hess and David Howard argue the cities sat on the boundary between Judahite and Danite territory, and were administratively shared or transferred. The Danite allotment in Joshua 19 was carved out of Judahite territory, since Judah's allotment turned out larger than necessary (Joshua 19:9). So Eshtaol and Zoreah were originally Judah's, then reassigned to Dan when the tribal apportionment was rebalanced. There's no contradiction — there's a historical sequence the narrative leaves implicit.

The rebalancing read has support in Joshua 19:9, which does state explicitly that Simeon's allotment was carved out of Judah's because Judah's portion was too big. The same logic could plausibly extend to Dan. The harder problem is that the text never actually says these specific cities were transferred. Joshua 15 and Joshua 19 each assigns them without acknowledging the other assignment. And the broader story of Dan in Joshua-Judges doesn't fit a clean transfer narrative. Judges 1:34 says "the Amorites forced the children of Dan into the mountain: for they would not suffer them to come down to the valley" — Dan failed to occupy its lowland allotment. Judges 18 then has the entire tribe of Dan migrating north and conquering Laish (renaming it Dan), abandoning the southern territory altogether. So the southern Danite allotment never actually functioned as a Danite territory historically.

The critical-scholarly read goes to the geography-list redaction problem. Joshua 13-21 contains some of the most heavily redacted material in the book, with multiple tribal boundary lists drawn from different sources and time periods. Yohanan Aharoni and Zecharia Kallai have argued the geographical lists in Joshua reflect administrative realities from different periods of Israelite history — pre-monarchic, Davidic, post-Solomonic — frozen into the text by editors who didn't reconcile them. The Judah list (Joshua 15) likely reflects a Judahite-administrative inventory; the Dan list (Joshua 19) reflects an older or competing tradition about Danite territorial claims. Eshtaol and Zoreah in Judges 13:25 and 16:31 (Samson's home territory) get treated as Danite, fitting Joshua 19. But the Judah inventory in Joshua 15 includes them too. The contradiction reflects competing administrative documents preserved by the redactor without harmonization. The transfer-theory works at the level of geography but isn't actually narrated; it's reconstructed by apologists to smooth a redactional seam.

contradictions.question: What tribe was Aijalon from?
contradictions.summary: Joshua 21:23-24 lists Aijalon as a Levitical city given out of the tribe of Dan, while 1 Chronicles 6:66, 69 lists Aijalon as a Levitical city given out of the tribe of Ephraim.
contradictions.commentary:
Two parallel Levitical-city lists, two different parent tribes for Aijalon. Joshua 21:23-24: "And out of the tribe of Dan... Aijalon with her suburbs, Gathrimmon with her suburbs." 1 Chronicles 6:66, 69: "The tribe of Ephraim... Aijalon with her suburbs, and Gathrimmon with her suburbs." The Chronicler is clearly working from a parallel source to Joshua 21 — the city pairings, the formula, even the suburb-language are nearly identical — but the parent tribe attribution differs.

The apologetic harmonization runs the historical-shift reading. Sara Japhet and Roddy Braun in their Chronicles commentaries argue that Aijalon was originally Danite (matching Joshua 21) but later transferred to Ephraim's territorial control after the Danite migration north (Judges 18). Since Dan effectively abandoned its southern territory, Ephraim absorbed the surrounding cities, and the Chronicler — writing centuries later — accurately reflects the post-Danite-migration administrative reality. So both texts can be true, just at different historical moments.

The migration-shift read has actual textual support. Judges 18 does narrate Dan's mass migration north, and the southern Danite cities did revert to neighboring tribes. 1 Chronicles 7:24 places Ephraim's territory in the area surrounding Aijalon. The Chronicler is well-known for updating geographical and administrative information from his sources to reflect later realities. So the reading isn't ad hoc.

Where it gets shakier is the textual-criticism dimension. The tribal lists in Joshua 21 and 1 Chronicles 6 are widely understood as variants of a single underlying source document. Sara Japhet's *I & II Chronicles* commentary in OTL and the textual notes in Steven McKenzie's commentary both observe that the two lists also disagree on the parent tribe of Gath-rimmon — Joshua 21:25 has it from the half-tribe of Manasseh while 1 Chron 6:69 (and apparently also the same context as Aijalon) has it from Ephraim. Plus the LXX of Joshua 21:24 has variants. So this isn't a clean "Joshua reflects period A, Chronicles reflects period B" sequence — it's two textually unstable lists with the kind of low-level corruption that scribal transmission of city-lists typically produces.

The critical-scholarly read combines both: the Levitical-city lists reflect an ideal program rather than continuously functioning administrative reality (Albrecht Alt, John Spencer), and the textual variants between Joshua 21 and 1 Chronicles 6 are partly real history (Dan's migration, Ephraim's expansion) and partly transmission errors. The contradiction is a real textual one even if the underlying administrative reality may have shifted; the historical-shift defense works in part but doesn't rescue the lists from being divergent witnesses to a fluid tradition.

contradictions.question: Who was Achan's father?
contradictions.summary: Joshua 7:1 names Achan as the son of Carmi, the son of Zabdi, the son of Zerah, but Joshua 7:24 and 22:20 call Achan "the son of Zerah" directly — collapsing what Joshua 7:1 presents as a four-generation lineage into a single father-son relationship.
contradictions.commentary:
The textual data is straightforward but generates a question of whether "son of" is being used literally or genealogically. Joshua 7:1: "For Achan, the son of Carmi, the son of Zabdi, the son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah." Joshua 7:24: "Joshua, and all Israel with him, took Achan the son of Zerah." Joshua 22:20: "Did not Achan the son of Zerah commit a trespass." 1 Chronicles 2:7 calls him "Achar, the son of Carmi" (with the spelling-variant Achar). The full pedigree in 7:1 puts Zerah three generations back; the shorter formulations call Zerah his father directly.

The apologetic harmonization is the standard *ben* ("son of") flexibility reading. Gleason Archer, Richard Hess, and David Howard point out that Hebrew *ben* is regularly used to mean "descendant of" rather than strictly "son of." Examples: Jesus called "son of David" (Matt 1:1), Jehu called "son of Nimshi" when Nimshi was actually his grandfather (1 Kings 19:16 vs. 2 Kings 9:2). On this reading, Joshua 7:24 and 22:20 are using *ben* in the descendant sense — Achan was descended from Zerah through Zabdi and Carmi — exactly as Joshua 7:1 specifies. There's no contradiction; just two levels of genealogical specificity.

The *ben*-flexibility argument is the consensus harmonization in scholarship across the spectrum. Hebrew *ben* does function as "descendant" frequently — standard reference grammars (Waltke and O'Connor; Joüon-Muraoka) and lexicons (BDB, HALOT) all document this. The genealogical convention of skipping generations was widespread in Ancient Near Eastern genealogies. So at the level of pure linguistic possibility, Joshua 7:24 calling Achan "son of Zerah" doesn't strictly contradict Joshua 7:1 listing Carmi as his immediate father. This contradiction is, frankly, on the weaker end.

That said, the critical-scholarly observation is that the inconsistency itself is evidence of editorial layering. Joshua 7:1 reads like a formal genealogical introduction (perhaps from a clan-list source); Joshua 7:24 and 22:20 read like narrative shorthand using the most prominent ancestor. Robert Boling and J. Alberto Soggin note that the Achan/Achar narrative shows multiple signs of redactional development, with clan-genealogical material being slotted into a shorter original narrative. The contradiction here is technically resolvable through the *ben*-flexibility reading, but the unevenness of the genealogical references still hints at composite origins. This one is more a candidate for "weak contradiction, mostly resolved by Hebrew lexicography" than a hard textual collision. It would be reasonable to recommend deletion or downgrade.

contradictions.question: Did Balak fight with Israel?
contradictions.summary: Joshua 24:9 says Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab, "arose and warred against Israel," but Judges 11:25 has Jephthah ask rhetorically — with implied answer "no" — whether Balak ever strove or fought against Israel.
contradictions.commentary:
Direct textual collision between two Deuteronomistic-history passages. Joshua 24:9: "Then Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab, arose and warred against Israel." The Hebrew verb is *wayyilachem* — "and he made war." Judges 11:25, in Jephthah's diplomatic letter to the Ammonite king: "Did he [Balak] ever strive against Israel, or did he ever fight against them?" The Hebrew verbs are *rov rav* and *nilchom nilcham* — emphatic infinitive-absolute forms of "strive" (Qal) and "fight" (Niphal), both negated by the rhetorical structure. The expected answer is "no." The Numbers 22-24 story of Balak corroborates Jephthah: Balak hires Balaam to curse Israel rather than meeting them in battle, then accepts the failed cursing and goes home. No combat is narrated.

The apologetic harmonization runs two directions. First, the broad-sense reading of *lacham*: Daniel Block and K. Lawson Younger argue "warred against" in Joshua 24:9 can describe hostile actions short of armed combat — diplomatic warfare, attempted cursing, hiring a prophet to spiritually attack Israel. Balak's hostility through Balaam counts as "warring" in the broader sense. Second, the partial-aggression reading: Trent Butler suggests Balak may have engaged in skirmishes not narrated in Numbers, and Joshua 24:9 preserves a tradition the Numbers narrator omitted.

The broad-sense reading is more textually defensible and is widely adopted across commentaries. Hebrew *lacham* does sometimes carry extended senses, and "warred against" describing the Balaam-cursing project isn't impossible. The context in Joshua 24:9-10 reinforces this — verse 10 says: "But I would not hearken unto Balaam; therefore he blessed you still: so I delivered you out of his hand." The summary is reading the entire Balak-Balaam episode as a hostile attack that YHWH frustrated. So Joshua 24:9-10 may be summarizing the Balaam attempt as "war" in the extended sense.

Where it gets harder is Jephthah's argument in Judges 11. Jephthah is making a legal-historical case to the Ammonite king that Israel never wronged Moab. His point depends on the proposition that Balak never actually engaged Israel militarily — that's why Jephthah uses *rov* (strive, contend in court) and *lacham* (fight) together, and answers in the negative. If Balak's Balaam-hiring counted as "warring," Jephthah's argument would collapse — the Ammonite king could simply respond "yes he did, that's exactly what Balak did with Balaam." The two passages use the same verb in incompatible senses for incompatible rhetorical purposes. The critical-scholarly read (Boling, Soggin) treats this as one of several internal Deuteronomistic-history inconsistencies where the redactor preserved competing summaries of the Balak tradition without harmonizing them. The broad-sense harmonization works for Joshua 24 alone but breaks Jephthah's argument in Judges 11.
